query: What streaming quantile selection algorithm should we implement (e.g., t-digest, GK, reservoir + selection), and what are its worst-case time, memory, and float32/64 numerical-stability guarantees?

response.query: What streaming quantile selection algorithm should we implement (e.g., t-digest, GK, reservoir + selection), and what are its worst-case time, memory, and float32/64 numerical-stability guarantees?
response.answer: For streaming quantiles, t-digest offers O(1) time, O(n) memory, and float32/64 stability. DDSketch provides O(1) time, O(log n) memory, and float32/64 stability. Reservoir + selection has O(1) time, O(k) memory, and float32/64 stability.

Title: There are two kinds: - quantile sketches, such as t-digest, which aim to control... | Hacker News
| |  | | --- | | fanf2 on July 25, 2024  | parent | context | favorite | on: My Favorite Algorithm: Linear Time Median Finding ...")   There are two kinds: - quantile sketches, such as t-digest, which aim to control the quantile error or rank error. These control the value error, and are generally easier to understand and faster than quantile sketches. Below I gave an algorithm I’ve used for quantile filtering, but that’s a somewhat different problem than streaming single-pass estimation of a stationary quantile. | | | |  | | --- | | ted\_dunning on July 26, 2024  | parent | next )   Most quantile sketches (and t-digest in particular) do not assume stationarity. T-digest gives you a strict bound on memory use and no dynamic allocation. It gives very good accuracy in practice and is very good at relative errors (i.e. 99.999th percentile estimate is between the 99.9985%-ile and 99.9995%-ile)  KL-sketch gives you a strict bound on memory use, but is limited to absolute quantile error. This is useless for extrema, but fine for medians)  Cormode's extension to KL-sketch gives you strict bound on relative accuracy, but n log n memory use. Exponential histograms give you strict bounds on memory use, no allocation and strict bounds on relative error in measurement space (i.e. 99.99%-ile ± % error). The exponential histogram is, by far, the best choice in most practical situations since an answer that says 3.1 ± 0.2 seconds is just so much more understandable for humans than a bound on quantile error. [2]  | | | |  | | --- | | throwaway\_2494 on July 25, 2024  | prev | next )   See also the Greenwald Khanna quantile estimator, an online algorithm which can compute any quantile within a given ϵ. | | | |  | | --- | | sevensor on July 26, 2024  | parent | next )   I am so glad I asked. I've used online quantile estimators (GK in particular) to very effectively look for anomalies in streaming data.

### your communities. ### more stack exchange communities. ##### Collectives™ on Stack Overflow. # On-line/Streaming algorithm for the selection of the top X percent of a time series. I am working on a time series of numeric values, such as those produced by a temperature sensor. The obvious solution of recording all samples and using any well-known algorithm for the extraction of the k-highest values is not possible in my case for two reasons:. I'd like this algorithm to be usable in real-time, or at least in a streaming mode with predetermined latency. Unlike this question, I do not need perfect accuracy, although I would like to be able to tune the parameters of the selection algorithm. Unfortunately all the VBR algorithms I studied are too focused on DSP and media streams for me to understand and/or implement. ## 2 Answers 2. At any time you have a small heap full of high items and a large heap full of low items, and you know whether the latest item was in the top 10% of those 10N. Note that if your samples rise steadily and then fall steadily over a period of time much larger than your 10N samples then nearly half the time the latest item will be in the top 10% - in fact it will be the largest item seen in the memory of 10N items. You cannot get high accuracy without storing the whole stream and knowing something about the distribution. Imagine a stream where the values are sorted in descending order. The 10% head of the list should be your answer but you have no idea how long the stream is so you have to store the whole stream because at any point it's possible that you processed less than 10% of the whole stream. If you have to store the whole stream you don't looking for an online algorithm anymore. A naive algorithm would be to chunk the stream to slices and calculate the top 10% of each slice. ## Your Answer. Thanks for contributing an answer to Stack Overflow! results.content: # Worst-case complexity. In computer science (specifically computational complexity theory), the **worst-case complexity** measures the resources (e.g. running time, memory) that an algorithm requires given an input of arbitrary size (commonly denoted as n in asymptotic notation). In the case of running time, the worst-case time complexity indicates the longest running time performed by an algorithm given *any* input of size n, and thus guarantees that the algorithm will finish in the indicated period of time. The order of growth (e.g. linear, logarithmic) of the worst-case complexity is commonly used to compare the efficiency of two algorithms. results.title: Randomized quicksort and selection algorithms | Intro to Algorithms Class Notes
results.content:
Title: Randomized quicksort and selection algorithms | Intro to Algorithms Class Notes
## 16.3 Randomized quicksort and selection algorithms. # 16.3 Randomized quicksort and selection algorithms. 1.3 Space complexity and algorithm efficiency. 1.4 Problem-solving strategies and algorithm design paradigms. 3.2 Selection Sort algorithm. 3.4 Comparison of elementary sorting algorithms. 4.2 Merge Sort algorithm and analysis. 4.3 Quick Sort algorithm and analysis. 5.3 Heap Sort algorithm and analysis. 8.2 Breadth-First Search (BFS) algorithm and applications. 8.3 Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithm and applications. 9.2 Kruskal's algorithm and implementation. 9.3 Prim's algorithm and implementation. 9.4 Comparison and analysis of Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms. 10.2 Dijkstra's algorithm and implementation. 10.4 Applications of shortest path algorithms. 14.4 Approximation algorithms for NP-complete problems. 16.1 Randomized algorithm design principles. 16.3 Randomized quicksort and selection algorithms. 16.4 Probabilistic analysis of algorithms. Randomized quicksort and selection algorithms shake up traditional sorting methods. By randomly picking pivot elements, these techniques avoid worst-case scenarios and achieve better average performance. These algorithms showcase the power of randomization in algorithm design. ### Randomization in Quicksort Algorithm. * Randomized quicksort introduces a probabilistic element by randomly selecting the pivot element. * Random pivot selection helps avoid worst-case scenarios (already sorted or reverse sorted arrays). * Modify partition function to randomly select pivot element using random number generator. * Simplifies algorithm analysis by focusing on expected-case rather than worst-case scenarios. * Calculate expected number of comparisons made by the algorithm. ## Randomization for Selection. ### Randomized Selection Algorithms. * Randomized QuickSelect applies random pivot selection principle from randomized quicksort. * Optimal for comparison-based selection algorithms. * Implement using techniques like reservoir sampling for efficient random selection in streams. * Utilize in algorithm design (median-based partitioning, approximate sorting). ## Randomized vs Deterministic Selection. ### Algorithm Comparison. * Deterministic selection (median-of-medians) guarantees worst-case O(n) time complexity. * Randomized selection provides expected O(n) time complexity. * Randomized algorithms generally simpler to implement (fewer lines of code, simpler logic). * Randomized selection performs well on average across all input distributions. * Deterministic algorithms may have specific input patterns triggering worst-case behavior. * Randomized selection preferred for simplicity and good average-case performance. * Space complexity: randomized O(logn) expected vs deterministic O(n) typically. * Use randomized selection with fallback to deterministic for difficult cases.

results.title: DDSketch: a fast and fully-mergeable quantile sketch with relative-error guarantees – the morning paper
results.content: # DDSketch: a fast and fully-mergeable quantile sketch with relative-error guarantees. DDSketch: a fast and fully-mergeable quantile sketch with relative-error guarantees Masson et al., *VLDB’19*. Officially in the paper DDSketch stands for ‘Distributed Distribution Sketch’ but that seems a bit of a stretch… surely it’s the ‘Datadog Sketch’ ! In putting together this write-up I’m grateful to the first author, Charles Masson, who gave a great talk on this paper at the VLDB conference and was kind enough to share his slides with me. This can play havoc with quantile sketches that are based on *rank error*. In this example, you can see that the GK-sketch, which uses rank error, is out by 1300ms compared to the ground truth. We want a fast-to-insert, fully mergeable (we can combine sketches in a distributed manner), space-efficient quantile sketch with relative error *guarantees*. ## One thought on “DDSketch: a fast and fully-mergeable quantile sketch with relative-error guarantees”.
